name: Syrah / Shiraz

lines.s10: Syrah is the savoury red of the northern Rhône, blackberry with cracked pepper and smoked meat, and Australia calls it Shiraz.
lines.s20: Syrah is the red grape of the northern Rhône, and in Australia it goes by the name Shiraz. From the Rhône expect blackberry, black olive and cracked pepper, and from the Barossa a fuller, riper wine with dark chocolate and vanilla.
lines.s45: Syrah and Shiraz are one grape under two names. Its home is the northern Rhône, on the steep river slopes of Hermitage and Côte-Rôtie. It is deep purple and tastes of blackberry, blueberry and cracked black pepper, often with a savoury note of black olive or smoked meat. It is medium to full bodied, with firm tannin, and usually aged in oak. The Rhône tends to be peppery and savoury, while Australian Shiraz is typically riper and richer, with chocolate and vanilla. Pour it with grilled lamb, venison or a peppered steak. Australia has grown it since 1832, and the Barossa still picks from vines planted in the 1840s.
lines.sale: Syrah brings blackberry with a savoury streak that few other reds have: cracked pepper, black olive and smoked meat. If the table is having lamb or anything from the grill, this is the bottle I would open.

glass.lead: Blackberry, blueberry and black plum cut with cracked black pepper, black olive and smoked meat, on a full, firm frame.

ladder.where: The northern Rhône, Hawke's Bay, Canberra and the Yarra Valley
Barossa Valley, McLaren Vale, Paso Robles and Stellenbosch

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity medium to medium plus, tannin medium plus to high, alcohol medium to high, body medium plus in the Rhône and full in the Barossa.

old.where: The northern Rhône: Hermitage, Côte-Rôtie, Cornas, Saint-Joseph and Crozes-Hermitage
old.glass: Tends to be savoury and perfumed more than sweet fruited: blackberry and blueberry with cracked black pepper, violet, black olive and smoked meat, at medium to medium plus alcohol, with fresh acidity and firm tannin.
old.cellar: Usually Syrah alone, though Côte-Rôtie may ferment up to 20 per cent Viognier with it; aged in French oak, often older or larger casks.

new.where: Barossa, McLaren Vale, Washington, California's Central Coast and Stellenbosch
new.glass: Typically riper, fuller and sweeter fruited, above all as Australian Shiraz: blackberry jam, blueberry and black plum with dark chocolate, liquorice and a lift of mint or eucalyptus, softer acidity and higher alcohol. Vanilla from new oak often shows.
new.cellar: Usually bottled under the grape's name, as Shiraz or Syrah; picked riper and often aged in new oak, in Australia long American and now often French.

contrast.why: The northern Rhône is near the cool limit for Syrah: slow ripening keeps pepper, acidity and moderate alcohol. Hotter, drier sites such as the Barossa ripen it fully, towards jam. The Rhône labels the place, the New World the grape.
contrast.blur: Cool sites such as Hawke's Bay, the Yarra Valley and the Sonoma Coast, and the old vines of the Swartland, make peppery, savoury wines; warm Rhône years give riper ones.
contrast.call: Black olive, smoked meat and pepper at moderate alcohol lean northern Rhône; chocolate, eucalyptus and vanilla on jammy fruit at higher alcohol lean Australia.

service.temp: 61 to 64 degrees Fahrenheit, 16 to 18 degrees Celsius: cool room temperature, never warm.
service.glass: A tall Bordeaux glass, with room to swirl.
service.decant: Consider it for a young, firm wine after tasting a sample; decant an old one off its sediment.
service.age: Most Shiraz is ready on release; northern Rhône and old vine wines reward five to twenty years.

with.why: the Rhône's own match, pepper against sweet fat
the wine's smoked meat note echoes the game
cracked pepper on the plate and in the glass
ripe Shiraz stands up to smoke and char

labels.means: The same grape under its Australian name; on a label it often signals a riper, fuller style.
Northern Rhône place names: the label names the hill or the village, and the grape is Syrah.
A blend of Grenache, Syrah or Shiraz and Mourvèdre, the southern Rhône recipe, common in Australia.
A different grape, also called Durif: an offspring of Syrah, darker and more tannic.

guest.q: Are Syrah and Shiraz the same grape?
guest.a: Yes, one grape. Shiraz is Australia's name for it, and on a label it usually promises a riper, fuller wine, where Syrah suggests a peppery, savoury one.

guest.q: Does Shiraz come from the city of Shiraz in Persia?
guest.a: It is a good story, but no. DNA work in the late 1990s found its parents to be two old grapes of south eastern France, Dureza and Mondeuse Blanche, so it began near the Rhône.

guest.q: Why does this wine smell of black pepper?
guest.a: Syrah makes the same aroma compound that gives peppercorns their scent. It shows most in wines from cooler sites and cooler years.

compare.tell: Malbec is plusher, with softer, rounder tannin and none of the savour; Syrah brings cracked pepper, black olive and smoked meat.
Cabernet Sauvignon shows cassis, cedar and a leafy edge on a more drying tannin; Syrah has cracked pepper, black olive and smoked meat.
Mourvèdre is gamier and more rustic, with heavier tannin and a note of leather; Syrah is more polished and peppery, with violet.

cards.front: Syrah: where is it at home, and who are its parents?
cards.back: The northern Rhône: Hermitage, Côte-Rôtie, Cornas, Saint-Joseph and Crozes-Hermitage. DNA work in the late 1990s found it a cross of Dureza and Mondeuse Blanche, two old grapes of south eastern France.

cards.front: Syrah blind: northern Rhône or Australian Shiraz, what tips it?
cards.back: Black olive, smoked meat, violet and pepper at moderate alcohol lean northern Rhône. Jammy blackberry, chocolate, eucalyptus and vanilla at higher alcohol lean Australia.

cards.front: Shiraz in Australia: when did it arrive, and which oak is traditional?
cards.back: In 1832 on most accounts, with vine cuttings brought from Europe. Barossa Shiraz was long aged in American oak, which gives vanilla and coconut; many cellars now use French oak.

questions.q: A guest loved a Barossa Shiraz last week and asks for the same grape in a more peppery, savoury style, with less sweetness of fruit. Which bottle do you bring?
questions.exp: Saint-Joseph is northern Rhône Syrah, typically peppery and savoury at moderate alcohol. McLaren Vale Shiraz is the same grape in the ripe style the guest already knows, and the other two are led by Grenache and Malbec.

questions.q: A blind red is opaque purple, with blackberry, blueberry, violet, cracked black pepper and a note of smoked bacon, on firm tannin and fresh acidity. Which grape is it most likely to be?
questions.exp: Black pepper and smoked meat with violet on a firm frame point to Syrah. Malbec shares the violet but lacks the pepper and the meat, and Cabernet Sauvignon shows cassis and cedar.

questions.q: A guest reads that the red Côte-Rôtie on the list holds a little white grape and asks which one. What do you tell her?
questions.exp: Côte-Rôtie may ferment up to 20 per cent Viognier with its Syrah, for perfume. Marsanne and Roussanne are the white grapes allowed in red Hermitage, not in Côte-Rôtie.

sources.title: Wine Australia: Shiraz, stories of Australian wine

report: Mode contrast, as the plan fixes it and as TASTE.world, both, requires. The Old World side is the northern Rhône and the New World side is led by Australian Shiraz, with Washington, California, Hawke's Bay and the Swartland named.
Say opens on the Court's own see-RAH and adds shih-RAZ, the Australian form; an American guest more often says shih-RAHZ.

The ladder has two rungs and no cool one, because the Court's grid reads the northern Rhône as moderate and Australia as warm. Hawke's Bay, Canberra and the Yarra Valley stand on the moderate rung beside the Rhône.
The Codex's records on Syrah read true and nothing here departs from them. The 20 per cent of Viognier in Côte-Rôtie and Syrah alone in Cornas are the Codex's own reviewed facts in the Rhône article.

The parentage, Dureza and Mondeuse Blanche, dated 1998, stands on Wine Grapes and on several pages read through search; some pages give 1999 for the publication. The Persian story is given as a story.
The arrival in 1832 stands on Wine Australia's own page; other pages date the collecting journey to 1831 and the arrival to 1832. The collector is not named because the fact does not need him.

The Barossa vines planted in the 1840s: the regional body's page and trade pages give 1843 for one vineyard, and one page records a dispute about the exact year, so the line says the 1840s and names no vineyard.
American oak as the long custom of Australian Shiraz and French oak as the newer choice is common trade teaching confirmed only in passing through search; a checker may wish a firmer source.
Lavender stands beside violet in the floral group on tasting notes of Syrah from the south of France and Washington; a checker may prefer violet with another note.
No Creole dish is given: none of the seven suits Syrah better than lamb, game or the grill.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.
